items.title: File:Canadian Copper Company acid converters.png
items.credit: The nickel industry; with special reference to the Sudbury region, Ontario, plate XLIX
items.desc: A set of the 10 Manhès-David acid converters (Allis-Chalmers type) operated by the Canadian Copper Company before 1911. The shell was 84 x 126 inches. If the starting matte was 36% Ni+Cu, the acid lining lasted 8 hours, or 7 tons of 80% Ni+Cu converted matte ; each blow lasting 1h 5min. If the starting matte was 30% Ni+Cu, the acid lining lasted 5.3 tons of converted matte ; each blow lasting 1h 1
items.cats: Manhès-David converters|PD US|PD Old|CC-PD-Mark|The Nickel Industry, With Special Reference to the Sudbury Region, Ontario (1913)|Canadian Copper Company nickel smelter

items.title: File:Canadian Copper Company basic converter.png
items.credit: The nickel industry; with special reference to the Sudbury region, Ontario, plate L
items.desc: Peirce-Smith converter built in 1911. The shell is 37 ft. 2 in. x 10 ft., with 44 tuyeres. It blows 60 tons of matte + 6 tons of quartz rock, wich are converted into 5-6 tons of converted matte. So, to fill the converter with converted matte, 300 to 400 tons of raw matte are added step by step, and blowed during a total time of 30 - 50 hours.

items.title: File:Flames evolution during blowing in a Manhès-David converter.png
items.desc: Evolution of the flame at the outlet of a Manhès-David converter during the blowing. We can notice the following steps : dark reddish-brown flame and heavy white fumes (oxydising of the secondary components) apple-green flamme (oxydising of the iron sulphide) white blueish flame (oxydising of the copper, with may slag in the converter) thin red-puple flame (oxydising of the remaing sulphur)
